B) Non-Contiguous Allocation
slides.notes: Now, let's understand how non-contiguous allocation works. Instead of placing a process in one continuous memory area, the operating system divides the process into multiple parts and stores them in different memory locations. Based on how this division is done, non-contiguous allocation uses techniques such as Paging, Segmentation, and Segmentation with Paging to manage memory efficiently.

slides.title: B) Non-Contiguous Allocation
slides.body:
Overcomes the limitations of contiguous allocation (fragmentation, need for large free block)
Offers flexibility, better memory utilization and support for large/multiple processes
Why It Matters?
slides.notes: Moving on, the main idea here is to avoid the restrictions of contiguous allocation. Instead of waiting for one large free memory block, the operating system can use the available free spaces efficiently. This makes memory management more effective, especially when multiple processes are running simultaneously.

B) Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation
Paging
slides.notes: Next, let's start with Paging. In this technique, the logical memory of a process is divided into fixed-size pages, while physical memory is divided into fixed-size frames of the same size. When the process is loaded into memory, each page is mapped to an available frame in physical memory. This allows the process to be stored efficiently without requiring one continuous block of memory.

slides.title: Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation
Pages vs Frames
Pages: These are logical divisions of a process. A process is divided into fixed-size pages.
The size of a page is determined by the OS and must be the same size for all pages in a process.
Frames: These are fixed-size blocks of physical memory.
The size of a frame matches the size of a page, ensuring that each page can be loaded into a frame without modification.
Relationship: Each page of a process is mapped to a frame in physical memory, but they don’t have to be contiguous. This means a process can be scattered throughout memory, improving memory utilization.

The size of a page is determined by the OS and must be the same size for all pages in a process.
Frames: These are fixed-size blocks of physical memory.
The size of a frame matches the size of a page, ensuring that each page can be loaded into a frame without modification.
Relationship: Each page of a process is mapped to a frame in physical memory, but they don’t have to be contiguous. This means a process can be scattered throughout memory, improving memory utilization.
Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation
Pages vs Frames

slides.body:
A process's pages don't need to be stored contiguously - they can be placed in any available frames scattered across physical memory
Main Benefit: Paging solves external fragmentation by allocating memory in fixed-size blocks (pages and frames), allowing processes to run efficiently on fragmented physical memory
Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation
Paging
slides.notes: Moving on, the pages of a process can be placed in any available frames, so they don't have to be next to each other in memory. Since all pages and frames are of the same size, memory can be allocated more efficiently, helping eliminate the problem of external fragmentation.

slides.title: Paging Solves This
slides.body:
Paging Solves This
Since pages and frames are fixed in size, the process can be allocated across non-contiguous frames, preventing external fragmentation and making better use of memory
External Fragmentation
This occurs when free memory is divided into small, scattered blocks that cannot fit a process
Paging
Solves External Fragmentation
slides.notes: Now, recall that external fragmentation happens when free memory is available but is scattered into small blocks. With paging, the operating system can place the process across multiple available frames instead of searching for one continuous space. This ensures memory is utilized effectively even when it is fragmented.

slides.notes: Now, let's trace the address translation process. The CPU first generates a Logical Address containing the Page Number and Offset. Here, the Page Number is P1, so the Page Table is consulted, which maps P1 to Frame F2. The Frame Number F2 is then combined with the same Offset to form the Physical Address. Finally, this address points to Frame F2 in Memory, where Page P1 is stored. This is how paging translates a logical address into the correct physical location while keeping the Offset unchanged.

slides.title: Physical Address = (Frame * Frame size) + Offset = (7 * 1024) + 512 = 7680 bytes
slides.body:
Physical Address = (Frame * Frame size) + Offset = (7 * 1024) + 512 = 7680 bytes
Logical → Physical Address Translation
Example 
Translation of a Logical Address
slides.notes: Now, let's work through a complete Logical Address Translation example. The Logical Address contains Page 2 and an Offset of 512. During the Page Table Lookup, Page 2 is mapped to Frame 7. The Physical Address is then formed by combining Frame 7 with the same Offset of 512. Assuming a Frame Size of 1024 bytes, the physical address is calculated as (7 × 1024) + 512 = 7680 bytes. This example shows that while the Page Number changes to a Frame Number, the Offset always remains unchanged.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body:
The Problem - Two Memory Accesses
Every memory reference in paging normally needs two trips to memory:
Read the Page Table Entry (to find the frame number)
Access the actual data at that frame
This doubles the effective time to access memory - a real performance cost
slides.notes: Moving on, one drawback of paging is that every memory request involves an extra step. Before accessing the actual data, the system must first check the Page Table to find the correct frame, which increases the overall memory access time.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Like looking up your friend's address in a phone book before visiting them—you first find the address, then go to the house. Similarly, paging first looks up the frame number in the page table and then accesses the actual data.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body:
Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
The TLB is a small, very fast hardware cache inside the CPU that stores recently-used Page Number → Frame Number translations
slides.notes: Now, to avoid checking the Page Table every time, the CPU uses a small, high-speed cache called the TLB(Translation Lookaside Buffer). It stores recently used page-to-frame mappings, allowing address translation to happen much faster.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body:
Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
On every memory reference, the MMU checks the TLB first:
TLB Hit
the frame number is found immediately in the TLB. No need to read the page table from memory. Fast path
TLB Miss
not found in the TLB. The MMU must look it up in the page table (in memory), and that result gets cached in the TLB for next time
slides.notes: Moving on, whenever a memory request is made, the MMU first checks the TLB. If the mapping is available, it's a TLB Hit and the frame is obtained instantly. Otherwise, it's a TLB Miss, so the system fetches the mapping from the Page Table and stores it in the TLB for future access.

slides.title: Effective Access Time (EAT)
slides.body:
Worked Example
Given:
TLB access time = 20 ns
Main memory access time = 100 ns
TLB hit ratio = 80%
slides.notes: Next, let's calculate the Effective Access Time (EAT) using this example. Here, the TLB takes 20 ns, main memory access takes 100 ns, and the TLB hit ratio is 80%. Using these values, we'll find the average memory access time.

slides.title: Effective Access Time (EAT)
slides.body:
Formula & Calculation
Formula
EAT = (hit ratio × (TLB time + memory time)) + (miss ratio × (TLB time + memory time + memory time))
Calculation:
On a hit: TLB (20ns) + one memory access (100ns) = 120 ns
On a miss: TLB (20ns) + page table access (100ns) + actual data access (100ns) = 220 ns
EAT = (0.8 × 120) + (0.2 × 220) = 96 + 44 = 140 ns
slides.notes: , plus one memory access to read the page table and get the frame number, plus a second memory access to actually fetch the data — that's why memory time appears twice on the miss sideNow, let's apply these values to the EAT formula. A TLB Hit takes 120 ns, while a TLB Miss takes 220 ns because of the additional page table access. Substituting the 80% hit ratio into the formula gives us an Effective Access Time of 140 ns.

slides.title: Effective Access Time (EAT)
slides.body:
What It Tells Us ?
A higher TLB hit ratio brings EAT closer to the TLB-hit cost (120 ns); a lower hit ratio pushes it toward the full miss cost (220 ns)
This is why TLB hit ratio is such a heavily optimized metric in real CPUs
slides.notes: Finally, the EAT mainly depends on the TLB hit ratio. A higher hit ratio keeps the access time closer to 120 ns, since most address translations are found directly in the TLB. On the other hand, frequent TLB misses require accessing the Page Table, increasing the access time toward 220 ns. This is why modern processors heavily optimize the TLB to improve overall memory performance.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body:
Advantages of Paging
Eliminates External Fragmentation
Memory is allocated in fixed-size frames, so there are no scattered unusable gaps between allocations
Simple to Implement
Allocation/deallocation just means tracking which frames are free or used
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at the advantages of Paging. Since memory is managed using fixed-size pages and frames, it eliminates external fragmentation, making memory utilization more efficient. Also, memory management becomes simpler because the operating system only needs to keep track of which frames are free and which are already allocated.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body:
Advantages of Paging
Efficient Memory Utilization
A process's pages can go into any available frames, so there's no need to find one large contiguous block
Memory Isolation
Each process has its own page table, keeping processes' memory cleanly separated
slides.notes: Next, Paging also improves memory utilization because a process can be loaded into any available frames, without requiring one contiguous memory block. In addition, each process maintains its own Page Table, which provides memory isolation and prevents processes from accessing each other's memory directly.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body:
Disadvantages of Paging
Internal Fragmentation
If a process's last page isn't completely full, that unused space inside the page is wasted
Page Table Overhead
Extra memory is needed to store a page table for every running process
slides.notes: Now, let's discuss some limitations of Paging. Since memory is allocated in fixed-size pages, the last page of a process may not be completely filled, leading to internal fragmentation. Also, every process requires its own Page Table, which consumes additional memory and adds some management overhead.

slides.title: Paging Mechanics
slides.body:
Disadvantages of Paging
Extra Memory Access
without a TLB, every memory reference needs two accesses: one to read the page table, one to read the actual data
No Logical Grouping
Unlike segmentation, pages don't correspond to a program's logical structure (code/data/stack)
slides.notes: Moving on, without a TLB, every memory request requires an additional lookup in the Page Table, increasing the overall access time. Another limitation is that pages are created based on a fixed size, so they don't represent meaningful program sections like code, data, or stack. This makes memory organization less aligned with the program's logical structure.

Segmentation is a memory management technique where a process is divided into variable-sized chunks called segments
Unlike paging, segmentation aligns with the user's logical view of a program, making memory management easier

Segmentation
slides.notes: Now, let's move to Segmentation. Instead of dividing a process into fixed-size blocks, it is split into variable-sized segments based on the program's logical parts, such as code, data, or stack. This makes the memory layout more meaningful and closely matches how a programmer views the program.

slides.notes: Now, let's understand the logical view of Segmentation. In Physical Memory Space, the segments A, B, C, D, and E are stored in different locations with free spaces in between, so they are non-contiguous. However, in the User Space, the program simply views them as independent logical segments, without worrying about where they are physically stored. These segments can represent different parts of a program, such as code, data, and stack, making memory management more natural and easier to organize.

slides.title: Segmentation
slides.body:
Segmentation
Analogy
slides.notes:
Think of a bookshelf with sections of different sizes for fiction, non-fiction, and journals.
 Each section is sized to fit its contents. Similarly, segmentation divides a program into logical, 
variable-sized segments like code, data, and stack, instead of fixed-size blocks like paging.

slides.title: Variable-sized divisions: Segments can have different lengths based on program r
slides.body:
Variable-sized divisions: Segments can have different lengths based on program requirements
Logical division of memory: Segments represent logical units of the program
Two-part address:
Segment Number (s): Identifies the segment
Offset (d): Specifies the exact location within that segment
Logical Address = ⟨Segment number, Offset⟩
Segmentation
Key Features
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the key features of Segmentation. Since segments represent logical parts of a program, they can have different sizes depending on their purpose. Also, every logical address consists of a Segment Number, which identifies the required segment, and an Offset, which locates the exact position within that segment.

slides.title: Protection and Sharing: Different segments can have access rights (read, write,
slides.body:
Protection and Sharing: Different segments can have access rights (read, write, execute) and can be shared among processes.
No internal fragmentation: Segments vary in size, avoiding wasted space within segments.
External Fragmentation: Can occur when free memory is divided into scattered blocks
Segmentation
Key Features
slides.notes: Moving on, Segmentation also provides better protection and sharing, as different segments can have different access permissions like read, write, or execute, and can even be shared across processes when required. Since segments are variable-sized, it avoids internal fragmentation. However, over time, external fragmentation can still occur because free memory gets scattered into smaller blocks.

slides.title: Segmentation
slides.body:
Segmentation
Segment Table
slides.notes: Now, to locate a segment in memory, the operating system uses a Segment Table. For each segment, it stores the Base Address, which tells where the segment begins in physical memory, and the Segment Limit, which defines the size of that segment. These values are used to translate a logical address into a physical address.

slides.notes: Next, let's understand how address translation happens in Segmentation. The CPU first generates a logical address consisting of the Segment Number and an Offset. The MMU uses the Segment Number to locate the required entry in the Segment Table and obtains the corresponding Base Address. It then adds the Offset to this Base Address to determine the exact physical address where the required data is stored.

slides.notes: Now, let's see how a Logical Address is translated into a Physical Address in Segmentation. The CPU generates a logical address containing the Segment Number (s) and the Offset (d). The Segment Number is used to access the Segment Table, which provides the Base Address and Limit of that segment. The operating system first checks whether d < Limit. If the condition is true, the Offset (d) is added to the Base Address to generate the Physical Address. Otherwise, the address is outside the segment's boundary, resulting in a Segmentation Fault.

slides.title: No Internal Fragmentation: Segments sized exactly to need (external fragmentatio
slides.body:
No Internal Fragmentation: Segments sized exactly to need (external fragmentation still possible)
Variable Segment Table Size: Depends on program structure, not always smaller than page table
Modular Loading: Only needed segments loaded, not entire program
Closer to User’s View: Matches the program’s logical structure (functions, arrays, etc.)
Security & Separation: Isolates sensitive data and operations for security
Segmentation
Advantages
slides.notes: Now, let's look at the advantages of Segmentation. Since segments are created according to the program's needs, internal fragmentation is eliminated, although external fragmentation may still occur. The Segment Table size depends on the program's structure, and only the required segments are loaded, supporting modular loading. Because segmentation reflects the program's logical structure, such as functions, arrays, code, and data, it is easier for programmers to understand and manage. Finally, separate segments can have different access permissions, providing better security and protection.

slides.title: Segmentation
slides.body:
Segmentation
Disadvantages
External Fragmentation: Free memory gets scattered, leading to wasted space
Overhead: Maintaining segment tables requires extra memory and management
Slower Access: Two memory lookups (segment table + memory) increase access time
Complexity: Managing variable-sized segments is more difficult than paging
Segmentation Faults: Occur when a program accesses memory outside its segment
slides.notes: Now, although Segmentation has several benefits, it also comes with some challenges. Since segments are variable-sized, free memory can become scattered over time, leading to external fragmentation. The operating system also needs to maintain a Segment Table and perform an additional lookup before accessing memory, which adds some overhead and slightly increases access time. Moreover, managing segments is more complex than Paging, and accessing data beyond a segment's limit results in a Segmentation Fault.

slides.notes: Finally, let's look at Segmentation with Paging, which combines the strengths of both techniques. Segmentation first divides the program into logical units such as Code, Data, Stack, and Heap. Then, instead of storing each segment as one continuous block, Paging further divides these segments into fixed-size pages, eliminating external fragmentation while still preserving the program's logical organization.

slides.title: Process Division
slides.body:
Process Division
A process is divided into four main segments
Code
Data
Stack
Heap
Segment Division
Each segment is divided into fixed-size pages, allowing for efficient memory usage
Segmentation with Paging
How it works?
slides.notes: Instead of directly dividing a process into pages, the operating system first separates it into logical segments like code, data, stack, and heap. Each segment is then divided into fixed-size pages. This combines the logical structure of segmentation with the efficient memory allocation of paging.

slides.title: Each segment has its own page table to map logical pages to physical frames
slides.body:
Each segment has its own page table to map logical pages to physical frames
The segment table stores the base address and limit of the segment’s page table
Page Table
Segmentation with Paging
How it works?
slides.notes: Moving on, after dividing each segment into pages, the operating system needs a way to track where those pages are stored. Each segment has its own page table, which maps the segment’s pages to physical frames. The segment table stores the location and size of each segment’s page table, helping the system find the correct page table during address translation.

slides.title: Address Translation
slides.body:
Address Translation
The CPU logical address is divided into:
Segment Number: Identifies the segment
Page Number: Identifies the page within the segment
Offset: Specifies the location within the page
Segmentation with Paging
How it works?

Page No

slides.notes: Next, let's see how the logical address is interpreted in this hybrid approach. Since both Segmentation and Paging are involved, the logical address is divided into three fields. The Segment Number first identifies the required segment, the Page Number locates the page within that segment, and finally the Offset pinpoints the exact location inside that page. This three-level addressing allows the system to preserve the logical structure while still benefiting from efficient page-based memory allocation.The operating system first uses the Segment Number to locate the correct page table, then uses the Page Number to find the corresponding frame, and finally combines that frame with the Offset to generate the Physical Address.

slides.title: Checks the segment table: Finds the base address of the page table
slides.body:
Checks the segment table: Finds the base address of the page table
Uses the page number: Locates the frame number
Combines with the offset: Forms the final physical address
The Memory Management Unit (MMU) follows this process
Segmentation with Paging
How it works?
slides.notes: Now, after the logical address is split, the MMU performs the translation in stages. It first refers to the Segment Table to locate the appropriate Page Table for that segment. Using the Page Number, it identifies the required frame, and finally combines the frame number with the Offset to generate the final physical address. This two-level lookup enables the system to leverage the benefits of both Segmentation and Paging.

slides.title: Combining segmentation and paging allows the system to benefit from both techniq
slides.body:
Combining segmentation and paging allows the system to benefit from both techniques:
Segmentation provides logical organization of memory, making the program structure more natural
Paging helps with efficient memory usage by dividing segments into fixed-size pages, reducing external fragmentation
Segmentation with Paging
Why Segmentation with Paging?
slides.notes:
Finally, neither Segmentation nor Paging is perfect when used alone. 
Segmentation makes programs easier to organize but can suffer from external fragmentation, 
whereas Paging uses memory efficiently but ignores the program's logical structure. By combining both, 
the system retains the logical view of a program while achieving efficient and flexible memory allocation.

slides.notes: Now, let's understand this with the example shown. The Segment Table contains the Base of PT and Limit for each segment. For instance, Segment 0 has a Base of PT = 512, which points to its own Page Table containing entries like Page 10 and Page 21. Similarly, Segment 1 points to a different Page Table with pages 19 and 52, while Segments 2 and 3 have their own page tables as well. This shows that each segment maintains an independent page table, making memory organization more modular and efficient.

slides.title: Since each segment has a page table, the page table is only created for the data
slides.body:
Since each segment has a page table, the page table is only created for the data of segments, reducing memory requirements
Reduced Page Table Size
Segmentation with Paging
Advantages
slides.notes:
Moving on, one advantage of this approach is that it avoids maintaining one large Page Table for the entire address space. 
Instead, each segment has its own Page Table, and memory is allocated only for segments that are actually used. This can reduce Page Table memory overhead.

slides.title: Segmentation provides a logical division (closer to how the program is written),
slides.body:
Segmentation provides a logical division (closer to how the program is written), while paging efficiently manages memory allocation
Programmer's View
Segmentation with Paging
Advantages
slides.notes:
Next, this approach is also more intuitive from a programmer's perspective. 
Developers naturally think in terms of code, data, stack, and heap, which are represented through Segmentation. 
Behind the scenes, Paging takes care of allocating memory efficiently, without affecting this logical organization.

slides.title: Combining segmentation with paging helps reduce external fragmentation compared
slides.body:
Combining segmentation with paging helps reduce external fragmentation compared to pure segmentation
Reduced External Fragmentation
Segmentation with Paging
Advantages
slides.notes: Now, one of the key benefits of this hybrid approach is the reduction of external fragmentation. Although the program is still organized into segments, memory is actually allocated in fixed-size pages. This means the operating system no longer has to search for one large continuous space for an entire segment, resulting in much more efficient memory utilization.

slides.title: Internal Fragmentation: Although external fragmentation is reduced, internal fra
slides.body:
Internal Fragmentation: Although external fragmentation is reduced, internal fragmentation can still occur within pages
Hardware Requirements: Extra hardware is needed to manage both the segment table and page table
Segmentation with Paging
Disadvantages
slides.notes: Finally, this hybrid approach also has a few trade-offs. Since memory is still allocated in fixed-size pages, some unused space can remain in the last page, leading to internal fragmentation. In addition, the system has to maintain both the Segment Table and Page Table, making the hardware and address translation mechanism more complex.

slides.title: Increased Memory Access Time: Translation involves multiple steps, making memory
slides.body:
Increased Memory Access Time: Translation involves multiple steps, making memory access slower compared to simpler paging or segmentation alone
Higher Memory Overhead: Maintaining both segment tables and page tables increases memory usage and makes memory management more complex
Segmentation-with-Paging
Disadvantages
slides.notes: Finally, this approach provides flexibility but increases complexity. Since the system needs to check both the Segment Table and Page Table before accessing data, address translation takes more steps and can increase access time. Maintaining both tables also requires extra memory.

slides.title: Comparison & Trade-offs
slides.body: Which One Wins?
slides.notes: Finally, there's no single memory management technique that is best in every situation. Paging is simpler and more efficient for memory allocation, while Segmentation provides better logical organization and protection. To balance these trade-offs, modern systems often use Segmentation with Paging, combining the strengths of both approaches while minimizing their individual limitations.
